question: What are the three main categories of immune system dysregulation?

options.D: Antibody production, cellular immunity, and innate defense

explanation: Immune system dysregulation broadly breaks down into overreaction, attacking self-tissues, and underperformance. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h1)

question: What usually causes immune system problems?

options.B: A single mutated gene passed down from parents
options.C: A mix of genetics, environment, and hormones

explanation: Most immune disorders don't happen from just one cause. Usually, a mix of internal factors (like your genes) and external things in your environment work together to trigger them. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for a severe, rapid anaphylactic allergic response?
explanation: Type I reactions are immediate, IgE-mediated responses that can quickly escalate to life-threatening anaphylaxis. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h2)

question: How are Type IV hypersensitivity reactions different from Types I, II, and III?

options.A: They only happen inside internal organs, never on the skin
options.B: They are driven by T-cells and take days to develop instead of using fast antibodies
options.C: They destroy red blood cells using complement proteins
options.D: They are only triggered by eating certain foods

explanation: Unlike the other types that rely on quick antibodies, Type IV is a 'delayed' reaction. It relies on T-lymphocytes taking a few days to show up and cause a reaction (like a bad rash). [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h2)

question: What do we mean by 'self-tolerance' in the immune system?

options.A: How fast white blood cells multiply during an infection
options.B: The capacity to destroy bacteria without causing inflammation
options.D: The ability to recognize and ignore the body's own healthy tissues

explanation: Self-tolerance is basically the immune system's way of knowing its own boundaries—it makes sure white blood cells leave our healthy cells alone instead of attacking them. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h3)

question: In type 1 diabetes, which part of the body does the immune system mistakenly attack?

options.A: The lining of the small intestine
options.B: Insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas

explanation: Type 1 diabetes is a classic autoimmune condition where the body turns on its own pancreas, destroying the beta cells that make insulin. Brilliant connection to remember! [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h3)

question: What is a primary immunodeficiency disorder?

options.A: Something that only affects adults over sixty
options.B: An issue triggered by common painkillers
options.C: An inherited genetic defect present right from birth
options.D: A condition caused by severe physical trauma later in life

explanation: Think of 'primary' as being born with it. These disorders stem from gene mutations passed down from parents, unlike secondary ones that happen later in life. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency?
explanation: HIV is acquired later in life. It slowly damages the immune system over time, which makes it a secondary immunodeficiency rather than something you are born with. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why does a recipient's immune system try to attack a newly transplanted organ?

options.A: It panics over the physical pressure of the new blood flow
options.B: It causes a sudden crash in red blood cells
options.C: It spots foreign human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) on the donor cells
options.D: It reacts badly to the surgical stitches

explanation: Our immune systems are super protective! When they see foreign HLA markers on a donor organ that don't match the body's own, they sound the alarm and try to reject it. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why do organ transplant patients need to take immunosuppressive drugs long-term?

options.A: To prevent high blood pressure after surgery
options.B: To stop the immune system from rejecting the new organ
options.C: To help the surgical wound heal much faster
options.D: To help the new organ pump its own blood

explanation: Immunosuppressants act like a quiet button for the immune system, keeping it calm so it doesn't recognize and destroy the precious new donor tissue. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h5)

question: Which lab test is commonly ordered first when checking for an autoimmune disorder?
explanation: The ANA test checks for antibodies that attack the nucleus of your own cells. It's a very common early screening tool for autoimmune conditions like lupus. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h6)

question: A patient keeps getting severe bacterial infections. Which lab values should the nurse check first to see how their antibody defenses are doing?

options.A: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen

explanation: Immunoglobulins (antibodies) handle our humoral immunity. Checking IgG, IgA, and IgM levels helps us see if an antibody shortage is leaving the patient wide open to infections. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why must patients with severe immunodeficiencies stay away from live vaccines?

options.A: The weakened germs in the vaccine can cause a real infection in a weak system
options.B: Live vaccines completely wipe out red blood cells
options.C: Live vaccines trigger severe allergies in everyone
options.D: The vaccine spoils easily at room temperature

explanation: Even though live vaccines use 'weakened' germs, a compromised immune system is too weak to fight them off—turning the vaccine into an actual infection. Safety first! [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h7)

question: What is the most important infection control habit for a nurse to teach a patient on immunosuppressive drugs?

options.B: Wearing heavy winter clothing outside at all times
options.D: Doing thorough and frequent hand hygiene

explanation: Never underestimate the power of clean hands! Proper hand hygiene is your patient's number one defense against picking up harmful germs in everyday life. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h7)
